lead: This unit teaches how to turn a physical system into a control model. You will compare open-loop and closed-loop control, derive transfer functions from differential equations, and simplify block diagrams and signal flow graphs. After it you can write the input-output transfer function of common mechanical, electrical, electromechanical, thermal, liquid-level and pneumatic systems.
about: This unit builds the model behind every control loop. Chapter 1.1 compares open-loop and closed-loop structures; 1.2 shows what feedback changes in gain, sensitivity, noise and stability. Chapter 1.3 introduces the differential-equation and transfer-function model. Chapters 1.4 to 1.7 apply it to mechanical, electrical-analogy, electromechanical, thermal, liquid-level and pneumatic systems. Chapter 1.8 reduces interconnected blocks, and 1.9 replaces the block diagram with a signal flow graph and Mason's gain formula. The aim is a single transfer function from a physical description, ready for time-response and stability work later.

chapters.idea: Open-loop control acts without measuring output; closed-loop control measures output and uses the error to correct it.
chapters.depth: Cover control-system terminology: plant, controller, sensor, actuator, reference, error, disturbance. Draw open-loop and closed-loop block diagrams, including unity negative feedback. Explain advantages and disadvantages of each. Some syllabi include SISO and MIMO labels and physiological examples such as body temperature; keep these brief. Mention two-position on-off action only as the simplest closed-loop action.

figure.aria: A closed-loop room heater: the sensor feeds room temperature back to the summing junction against the target of 25°C.

chapters.example: A room heater raises room temperature at 0.5°C/min when on. Open-loop: switch on for 20 min starting at 20°C. Closed-loop: thermostat target 25°C, sensor checks every 1 min, heater on while T < 25°C. Find final temperature and heater on-time in each case, assuming no cooling.
chapters.trap: Calling a system closed-loop just because it has a controller; without a sensor feedback path it is open-loop. Also watch the summing-junction sign.
chapters.leave: Feedback effects go to 1.2, block reduction to 1.8, time response to Unit 2, controller actions to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Negative feedback reduces the effect of parameter changes and disturbances by sacrificing forward gain.
chapters.depth: Derive A = G/(1 + GH) for negative feedback. Define loop gain GH, sensitivity S = 1/(1 + GH), and desensitivity. Show dA/A = S dG/G. Discuss effect on overall gain, bandwidth, noise, disturbance rejection and stability; feedback can improve or degrade stability, tested in Unit 3. Positive feedback appears only as contrast. Some syllabi call sensitivity the fractional change ratio.

figure.aria: A negative-feedback loop with forward gain 100 and feedback factor 0.1; the feedback path returns to the summing junction with a minus sign.

chapters.example: For a negative-feedback loop with forward gain G = 100 and feedback factor H = 0.1, find closed-loop gain A and sensitivity S. If G increases by 10%, estimate the percentage change in A.
chapters.trap: Using 1 + GH when the summing sign is positive; forgetting S is with respect to G and that feedback reduces gain but does not make output exactly follow input.
chapters.leave: Stability criteria to Unit 3, controller design to Unit 5, detailed noise analysis to advanced texts.

chapters.idea: A linear time-invariant system is modelled by a differential equation, and its transfer function is the Laplace ratio of output to input with zero initial conditions.
chapters.depth: Use only the Laplace transform needed for differentiation. Define G(s) = Y(s)/U(s), LTI, zero initial conditions, poles, zeros and characteristic equation. Distinguish proper and strictly proper. Convert ODE to transfer function and back. Mention a MIMO transfer matrix in one line; state space belongs to Unit 6. Some syllabi call this the input-output model.

figure.aria: Two rows show the same system: a time-domain ODE and its Laplace transfer function G(s) = 4/(2s²+3s+1).

chapters.example: A system obeys 2y″(t) + 3y′(t) + y(t) = 4u(t), with zero initial conditions. Find the transfer function and its poles.
chapters.trap: Leaving initial-condition terms in the Laplace transform; treating a nonlinear or time-varying equation as a transfer function.
chapters.prereq: 1.1–1.2 for the input-output idea; basic calculus and Laplace transform.
chapters.leave: State-space models to Unit 6; time response to Unit 2; stability to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Mechanical translational and rotational systems are modelled by Newton's second law and its rotational analogue, giving mass-spring-damper equations.
chapters.depth: Translational: mass m (kg), viscous damper c (N·s/m), spring k (N/m), displacement x (m), force F (N); use free-body diagrams and ΣF = m x″. Rotational: inertia J (kg·m²), torsional damper b (N·m·s/rad), torsional spring kt (N·m/rad), angle θ (rad), torque T (N·m); use ΣT = J θ″. Build transfer functions with zero initial conditions. Include gear inertia reflection only if listed. Some syllabi call c the damping coefficient.

figure.aria: A tree splits mechanical systems into translational elements with example values and rotational elements with symbols.

chapters.example: For a mass m = 2 kg on a horizontal surface, spring k = 8 N/m and damper c = 2 N·s/m, an external force F(t) acts. Neglect friction and find X(s)/F(s).
chapters.trap: Wrong sign on spring or damper forces; mixing translational and rotational units; forgetting that x is in metres and θ in radians.
chapters.leave: Electrical analogies to 1.5; electromechanical coupling to 1.6; state space to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Mechanical systems can be represented by equivalent electrical circuits using force-voltage or force-current analogy, so circuit methods give the same transfer function.
chapters.depth: Force-voltage (F-V): force↔voltage, velocity↔current, displacement↔charge, mass↔inductance, damper↔resistance, spring↔1/capacitance. Force-current (F-I): force↔current, velocity↔voltage, displacement↔flux linkage, mass↔capacitance, damper↔conductance, spring↔1/inductance. Show an element table and build the analogous circuit for a given mechanical system. Some syllabi call these direct and inverse analogies.

figure.aria: Three mechanical elements m = 2, b = 3 and k = 4 map by the force-voltage analogy to L = 2 H, R = 3 Ω and C = 0.25 F.

chapters.example: A translational system has m = 2 kg, b = 3 N·s/m, k = 4 N/m. Using the force-voltage analogy, find the equivalent inductance, resistance and capacitance.
chapters.trap: In the F-V analogy the spring maps to 1/C, not C; in the F-I analogy the damper maps to conductance, not resistance.
chapters.prereq: 1.4 for mechanical elements; basic circuit laws.
chapters.leave: Circuit analysis details to electrical engineering; transfer-function derivation is already in 1.3.

chapters.idea: An electromechanical servomotor couples an electrical armature circuit to a mechanical load through torque and back emf.
chapters.depth: Armature-controlled DC motor: va = R i + L di/dt + Kb ω; torque T = Kt i; load J dω/dt + b ω = T; θ′ = ω. Derive θ(s)/Va(s) with zero load torque. Define Kt (N·m/A), Kb (V·s/rad), J, b, R, L. Mention AC and two-phase servomotors in one line; only a few universities teach detailed AC servo models. Some syllabi call this actuator modelling.

figure.aria: A DC servomotor block diagram: armature voltage drives torque, the load gives speed, 1/s gives angle θ, and Kb s feeds back back-emf.

chapters.example: An armature-controlled DC motor has R = 1 Ω, L = 0.1 H, Kt = 0.5 N·m/A, Kb = 0.5 V·s/rad, J = 0.01 kg·m² and b = 0.1 N·m·s/rad. Find θ(s)/Va(s) with no load torque.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the back-emf term Kb s θ(s); using speed ω(s) when the output is angle θ(s), which adds a factor s.
chapters.leave: Motor control and power electronics to later courses; state-space motor model to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Thermal, liquid-level and pneumatic systems obey conservation and resistance-capacitance laws, often giving first-order transfer functions.
chapters.depth: Thermal: heat capacity Ct (J/°C), thermal resistance Rt (°C/W), qin = Ct dT/dt + (T − Ta)/Rt; first-order transfer function. Liquid level: tank area A (m²), linear outflow q = h/R with R (s/m²), A dh/dt = qin − h/R; H(s)/Qin(s) = R/(AR s + 1). Pneumatic: pressure-flow resistance and volume capacitance, small-signal linear model. Mention nonlinearity and linearization only. Some syllabi call these process models.

figure.aria: A liquid-level loop: inflow 0.1 m³/s fills a tank of area 2 m², level h returns through resistance R = 5 to the summing junction.

chapters.example: A tank has area A = 2 m² and linear outflow qout = h/R with R = 5 s/m². Inflow is a step qin = 0.1 m³/s. Find H(s)/Qin(s), the time constant and final level.
chapters.trap: Using gauge pressure or temperature without a consistent reference; forgetting that the liquid-level model is linear only for small changes around an operating point.
chapters.leave: PID process control to Unit 5; nonlinear tank dynamics to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Block diagram reduction replaces interconnected blocks by one transfer function using series, parallel and feedback rules.
chapters.depth: Give rules for series, parallel, feedback, moving a summing point ahead or behind a block, moving a take-off point, and eliminating a feedback loop. Emphasize summing-junction signs and canonical negative feedback. Some syllabi call this block diagram algebra. Keep signal flow graphs for 1.9.

figure.aria: A negative-feedback block diagram with G1 = 2/(s+1), G2 = 3/(s+2) in series, unity feedback, and output C(s).

chapters.example: Reduce the negative-feedback block diagram with G1 = 2/(s+1), G2 = 3/(s+2) in series and H = 1. Find C(s)/R(s).
chapters.trap: Ignoring the minus sign at the summing junction; moving a take-off point without adding the same factor to the branch.
chapters.leave: Signal flow graphs and Mason's formula to 1.9; stability to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A signal flow graph is a directed graph of the same equations, and Mason's gain formula gives the transfer function by counting forward paths and loops.
chapters.depth: Define nodes, branches, branch gains, source and sink. Define forward path gain Pk, loop gain Li and non-touching loops. Use Δ = 1 − ΣLi + ΣLiLj − … and path cofactor Δk. Apply T = (ΣPkΔk)/Δ. Convert the block diagram from 1.8 to a signal flow graph. Some syllabi call this Mason's rule. Keep multiple-loop counting careful.

figure.aria: A signal flow graph with forward path R to E to X to C and one feedback loop from C to E with gain −H.

chapters.example: For the block diagram with G1 = 2/(s+1), G2 = 3/(s+2) and H = 1, draw the signal flow graph and use Mason's gain formula to find C(s)/R(s).
chapters.trap: Adding touching loops as if non-touching; using Δk = 1 when the forward path touches a loop; sign errors in loop gains.
chapters.leave: State-space signal flow graphs to Unit 6; stability from the characteristic equation to Unit 3.
